items.why: Tests Jeroboam’s continued wrongdoing by contrasting what he refuses to change with what he does again.
The unanchored “he” blurs the original messenger with the father repeating the message.
Distinguishes the group’s victory over all four descendants from Jonathan’s individual killing.
Requires tracking the officer through the dialogue to identify whose predicted death occurs.
Clearly distinguishes the sons who saddle the donkey from the old prophet who rides it.
Tests the substantive difference between the covenant including the Lord and the covenant between king and people.
Tests the next narrated event rather than directly distinguishing Jotham’s earlier governance from his accession.
Distinguishes Uzziah’s stated reason for leaving from the priests’ action of hurrying him out.
Treats the king’s suspected ambush plan as the Arameans’ established intention.
Clearly contrasts the men’s chosen surrender with entering the famine-stricken city.
Asks only which separately narrated battle comes first, rather than testing who kills whom.
The key “the news” never identifies the report’s content, so it provides no substantive comprehension criterion.
Clearly distinguishes the king issuing the seizure order from the man targeted by it.
Identifies Uzziah as the temple entrant rather than confusing him with the priests following him.
Requires following the quoted speaker’s perspective to distinguish the two children’s planned days.
Distinguishes Zechariah’s teaching role from Amaziah’s role as an example of right conduct.
Separates Elisha’s warning to the doubter from his earlier prediction about food prices.
Tests the central motive for refusal: obedience to the Lord’s command, not dissatisfaction with the offer.
The order is clear, but the question mainly tests the last activity in a narrated list.
The unqualified “first” rewards the order of a military-action list rather than an important distinction.
Distinguishes Jehoiada’s distribution of the weapons from David’s prior ownership.
Clearly distinguishes the accusers ordered to present their case from the council that previously heard it.
The stated purpose of making Uzziah king is distinct from the circumstance of his father’s death.
Separates the family leaders’ command role from the officers’ role in mustering the army.
Tests the crucial participant shift from the prophet saddling the donkey to the man of God departing.
Repeats the officer-trampling identification, with a shorter and easier pronoun link.
The three on-duty companies also guard the temple, so the keyed group is not an exclusive answer.
Uses the letter’s sender–recipient format to distinguish Claudius Lysias from Governor Felix.
Distinguishes the Philistine killed from David, the person Abishai rescues.
Tests the men’s consequential decision to share the news instead of continuing to conceal their gains.
Keeps the young messenger distinct from Paul, who arranges his meeting with the commander.
The report marks a meaningful transition to plundering, though the stem tests only immediate narrative order.
Attributes the farming motive to Uzziah rather than to the workers employed in his fields.
Requires identifying the eaten child through the reporting mother’s “my son,” rather than the other woman’s hidden son.
Distinguishes the king requesting healing from the man of God who intercedes.
Distinguishes the three named opponents from the Ammonites who bring tribute.
The city and tomb are nested destinations, making “first” an artificial distinction between overlapping locations.
The needless phrase “Ahaziah’s son’s nurse” makes a simple identity question cumbersome and indirect.
Tests the stated cause of the city’s calm rather than the parallel reaction of rejoicing.
Separates the centurions receiving the order from the soldiers they must assemble.
Distinguishes the imagined attackers from the king believed to have hired them.
Distinguishes the king ordering the killing from the messenger sent to carry it out.
Correctly frames the angel story as a claim and tests whom its instruction concerns.
Connects Paul’s extended speech to his planned departure rather than an unrelated room detail.
Tracks the escort’s split: the soldiers return while the cavalry continue with Paul.
Identifies the beaten exorcists as those who flee, not the man who attacks them.
Illnesses also disappear, so excluding them depends on matching “leaves” to the exact verb rather than understanding the healing.
Separates the commander meant to deliver Paul from the council requesting his appearance.
Generic “assembling materials” obscures the scrolls and turns their public destruction into an action-order test.
The instructions also presume the woman’s execution, so excluding her relies narrowly on the word “sword.”
Separates the noise that draws Athaliah there from what she sees after arriving.
Consent is explicitly awaited, but “act” leaves the relevant stage of the ambush plan underspecified.
The judgment’s recipient is identifiable, but “whose body is warned” is grammatically awkward.
Distinguishes Josiah, the predicted future killer, from Jeroboam standing at the altar in the present scene.
